analysis.title: US CPI: October preview
key_insights: CACIB expects October headline CPI at 0.29% MoM SA. No YoY estimate is given because the BLS never published the October 2025 index (government shutdown). The fixings market, using an arbitrary 325.604 reference index for October 2025, marks October 2026 YoY at 3.56%, and CACIB is 2bp above that.
CACIB expects core CPI at 0.26% MoM SA in October, vs 0.29% in August (boosted by noise in telephone services) and 0.33% in September. This is 2bp above the 0.24% Bloomberg average consensus.
The 3M moving average of core, annualised, would reach 3.53% in October, the highest since January 2025. CACIB calls the report relatively benign, with core back around 0.25% MoM SA.

Using gasoline and natural gas futures as energy inputs, and given the recent sharp decline in Brent, CACIB's model suggests headline CPI around 3.5-3.6% YoY until February next year. The peak was 4.25% YoY in May 2026.
CACIB sees very limited second-round effects from higher energy prices due to the Iran war, aside from airfares. Some pass-through is starting in core goods, but nothing significant yet.

Base effects will dominate core YoY for the next six months. Fading 2025 tariffs pull core goods YoY lower. OER and rent YoY will be abnormally strong from November 2026 to March 2027 because of the BLS methodology choices after the 2025 shutdown.
CACIB expects core CPI to run around 2.8-2.9% YoY until February 2027, then ease toward 2.5% by end-2027. It averages 2.6% YoY so far this year.

Services are forecast at 0.25% MoM SA in October, below August (0.33%) and September (0.37%). Airfares are forecast at +1.48% MoM SA and OER at +0.31%. Hotels are forecast at -1.33% and internet services at -0.8%.

Core goods are forecast at 0.25% MoM SA, driven by education and communication commodities (+0.4%, with chipset and memory prices) and recreation commodities (+0.51%, from higher input costs such as plastics, shipping and logistics). CACIB expects core goods near 1% YoY until about mid-Q2 2027 and about 0.4% YoY at end-2027.

Food is forecast at +0.34% MoM SA, with cereals and bakery at +0.70% and meats, poultry, fish and eggs at +0.07%. CACIB expects food CPI near 3% YoY in coming quarters and about 3.5% going into Q4 2027 and Q1 2028, with El Nino as an upside risk.

Energy is forecast at +0.57% MoM SA (-0.63% NSA). Motor fuel is -0.75% NSA, electricity -0.9% and natural gas +0.6%. Energy YoY peaked at 23.5% in May 2026 and was 20.5% in September. CACIB expects 17-20% until February 2027, then a return to about 0% as the March and April 2025 moves leave the sample.

The October PPI, released 13 November, will be used to finalise core PCE forecasts. A methodology change in late September removed portfolio management and investment advice from the relevant PCE components. It was revised down to 8.6% YoY in July from 20.8%, which alone cut more than 0.2ppt off core PCE YoY.
Core PCE is 3.1% YoY, more than a full percentage point above target. If CACIB's forecast is right, October CPI would improve on September but still be firmer than ideal for the Fed.

CACIB expects the Fed to hike 25bp in December and another 25bp in March, for 75bp of hikes in total to reverse last year's insurance cuts, at an every-other-meeting pace, then pause. The downward PCE revisions likely bought the Fed time to hold in October.

Fedspeak supports a gradual tightening path. Williams, Jefferson and Waller had been supportive before October. Dallas Fed's Logan, who dissented in favour of a hike in July, backed a gradual approach after the October meeting.

risk_factors: Core CPI could come in above CACIB's 0.26% MoM SA forecast and the 0.24% consensus, which would add to the case for tightening.
Food CPI faces upside risk from El Nino and from fertiliser and fuel price pass-through.
Higher imported and logistics costs from the energy crisis could keep core goods inflation firmer than the tariff base effects imply.
Telephone services and hotels have been erratic, adding noise to monthly core prints.
Lower immigration is potentially inflationary through labour supply, while AI is potentially deflationary medium term. CACIB does not expect either to dominate the next year.
vol_and_positioning: The US fixings (inflation swap) market marks October 2026 headline CPI YoY at 3.56% using an arbitrary 325.604 reference index. CACIB is 2bp above that.
geopolitical: Iran war and the energy crisis it caused: higher energy and imported costs, with airfares the main second-round effect in core CPI.
Impact of the midterm election 'blue wave' on CPI: CACIB expects no major effect beyond lower crude prices already in its model.
2025 US government shutdown: the BLS never published the October 2025 index, which prevents a YoY estimate for October 2026 and distorts OER and rent YoY from November 2026 to March 2027.
